explanations.explanation: This neuron is a detector for unusual Unicode‐encoded symbols—especially the “replacement character” (�) and other high–codepoint/non-ASCII glyphs that show up when text contains mis-decoded bytes or non-Latin scripts.

This feature flags the boundary tokens of standalone titles or section headings (e.g. the initial capitalized word or the trailing punctuation of a blog‐post title, product heading, article section header, etc.).

This feature fires on the literal “.” used as a structural separator in formal identifiers—most prominently the dot in HTML/DTD version strings (e.g. “4.01” or “1.0” in DOCTYPE declarations) and similar period-delimited codes or abbreviations (e.g. “U.S.,” “No. 99-41374”) within mark-up and legal-text contexts.
This feature fires on the very first word of a new section, heading or article—typically a title-case token (often a proper name) that marks the start of a news/encyclopedic entry or subsection.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on tokens that begin key semantic chunks in formal or structured text—e.g. the leading word in an instruction (“the” in “Remove the …”), the head of a license or contributor name (“Perm” in “Permissive License,” “Dre” in “Drepper”), the initial segment of an identifier or XML attribute (“To” in “fileID ToRecycleName,” “Are” in “SafeAreas,” “M” in “MPL”), or the first token of a named entity or domain (“P” in “CM Punk,” “.” in “glassfish.dev”). In short, it detects chunk-initial markers—starts of commands, names, license clauses or code/metadata fields—in technical and legal boilerplate.

This feature lights up on the little “framing” markers you see around file‐ or section‐level metadata and annotations—things like comment‐block delimiters (/*…*/), include‐guard macros, license/copyright headers, Markdown/BibTeX bold or annotation markers (**…** or @…{}), section separators (%…), config stanzas, etc. It’s essentially a detector for the punctuation and symbols that open or close metadata/annotation blocks across code and markup.

This feature is basically a “section-boundary/boilerplate” detector.  It lights up on the tokens that open or close metadata or comment blocks (e.g. “/*”, the leading “*” lines in C‐style comments, “*/”), on import/include or @charset lines, on license-copyright headers, and more generally on the start or end of structured headers or field names in both code and prose (InfoPlist keys, section titles, dates, etc.).

This neuron fires on standalone BPE tokens that correspond to high-level “metadata” or structural markers—whole words or subwords that often kick off headers, CTAs, dates, names, URLs, IDs, etc. (e.g. “Find,” “In,” “Salt,” “May,” “www,” “url,” month names, numbers like “18,” hex/ID characters like “L”/“e”/“ud,” punctuation pairs “((,” and so on).

The feature flags enumeration boundaries in formal/technical prose—i.e. the tokens (conjunctions like “and,” possessive markers/apostrophes, hyphens in codes or citations) that join or separate items in lists, series, coordinate phrases or structured references.

This feature fires on the very first digit of any segmented numeric literal—e.g. the leading “1” or “0” in version strings, decimals, percentages, coordinates, etc.—marking the start of a new numeric segment after a separator (dot, dash, bracket, etc.).

This feature fires on the little “metadata” markers that open or close formal headers and footers in text—namely proper‐name tokens (case titles, people, places, orgs), common abbreviations (months, “U.S.,” initials), and the punctuation that signals bylines, headlines, dates, legal citations or copyright/license notices.

This feature flags the little “glue” punctuation in code identifiers and member/index expressions—things like underscores in snake_case, dots in attribute or schema qualifiers, hyphens in names, bracket‐accessors (and even percent‐operators)—i.e. the separators that stitch together multi-part names or accessors across many programming languages.

This neuron detects document‐structure markers—e.g. section headings and titles formatted via all-caps words, repeated punctuation or Markdown syntax (######, ==== underlines), separators, etc.—rather than lexical content.

This feature specializes in spotting structural-boundary tokens in formal text—most often uppercase abbreviations ending in a period (e.g. month and state abbreviations in datelines like “Dec.” or “Minn.,” company suffixes like “Inc.,” reporter citations like “F.3d”), as well as the final word of headlines or section headings.
This feature fires on tokens that kick off a new document or section header—i.e. the very first word/character of titles, abstracts, code‐block labels or other headings—across languages and genres.

This neuron lights up on the little “glue” bits that hold text or code together—short, high-frequency tokens (prepositions like of/at/off, small numerals like 2/6/25/hundreds, tiny identifiers or keywords such as end/inf/preg/JECT, and brief names). In other words, it marks the connective or indexing elements that structure prose, metadata and code.

This neuron is a “heading/title” detector – it spikes on the characteristic boundary words and punctuation (dates, leading capitals, ending periods or numbers, etc.) that mark the start or end of article and section titles (news headlines, Wikipedia headers, press‐release titles, etc.).

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a “literal‐terminator” detector: it spikes on the boundary token that closes a literal span—whether that’s the leading digit in a decimal number (e.g. the “0” in “0.22%” or the “1” in “1.000000”) in a scientific context, or the closing delimiter (quote or angle-bracket) at the end of a C/C++ include path.
This feature lights up on block‐level header or boilerplate metadata lines—e.g. license-comment banners in source files and docket/citation headings in legal opinions.

This feature lights up on the little “glue” words and list-markers that signal relationships or enumerate content in formal expository text—prepositions like “of,” “in,” inclusion verbs/adverbs (“include,” “including,” “offers,” “included,” “Additionally”) and list-intro punctuation (colons)—all of which introduce attribution, location, membership or additional items.

This neuron fires on the little “boundary” marks that close off top‐level headers or metadata lines across genres – the final dot/period (or similar punctuation) at the end of a title, dateline, DOCTYPE version, PHP-tag opener, etc., signaling the transition from a document’s header/block label into its main body.

This neuron specializes in spotting top-of-file import/include directives across languages—i.e. lines like  
  • C/C++  #­include “foo.h” or <foo.hpp>  
  • C#    using Namespace;  
  • Go    import "pkg"  
and so on—firing most strongly on the closing delimiter (>, ", or ;) that ends those inclusion statements.
This neuron detects sentence- or segment-final delimiters (essentially the “.” or equivalent end-of-line marker) that signal the boundary of a sentence or block across languages and contexts.
This neuron fires whenever a token is the start of a fresh word/subword (i.e. it carries a leading‐space or punctuation prefix in BPE), signaling a word boundary.

This feature detects the standardized “top‐of‐document” boilerplate or metadata header—e.g. the uppercase legal case headings (“IN THE UNITED STATES…COURT OF APPEALS…”) or code‐license comments (“Copyright…, Licensed under the Apache/GNU/BSD License…”) that appear at the very start of judicial opinions or source files.

This neuron is a marker for English discourse connectives—especially subordinating prepositions/conjunctions and adverbials (Before, after, on, despite, etc.) that introduce temporal or contrastive clauses.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees the “�” replacement glyph (U+FFFD) or similarly garbled/unknown‐symbol tokens—i.e. it flags mis-encoded or unrecognized characters (across languages, code, markup, etc.).

This neuron fires on the very last token of a title, header or metadata line—marking the boundary that closes section‐titles, comment‐block banners or import/“generated by” directives across code and prose.

This feature fires on the boundary before a file‐ or module‐level directive or declaration – things like imports/using statements, includes/macros, package or namespace lines, exports/defines, license headers, etc. In other words, it tags the start of a new top-level section in code or metadata.

This neuron fires on discourse‐linking function words—i.e. conjunctions and connectives (however, meanwhile, but/yet, because, that, whether, like, to, etc.) that signal logical or rhetorical relations (contrast, cause, condition, comparison, subordination) between clauses.

This neuron fires on the little “end‐of‐unit” punctuation or delimiters you see everywhere in code- and doc-style text—full-stops in acronyms or at the end of headers, copyright and license notices, date/month abbreviations, short update titles, XML/HTML tags’ closing “>”, include-paths, etc. In other words, it marks structural boundary punctuation that terminates names, metadata lines or small code snippets.

This neuron lights up on the little “glue” words and adverbs people use to link or shift between clauses—things like and, then, also, finally, sorry, worry, know (often right after a comma). In other words, it detects informal discourse‐transition markers in online text.

This feature fires on high‐level “header” or metadata markers that introduce or label major document or code sections—e.g. legal captions and docket headings (“People v. …”, court names, record impound notices), section titles (“Biographical Information,” “Page”), file-level declarations in code (“import …”, “package …”), copyright/license headers, etc.

This neuron fires on the head of multi-word noun compounds—often technical, legal or product names (e.g. “heat dissipation,” “plasma arc cutting,” “radar gun,” “ammonium sulfate,” “liquor license,” “handcrafted tea”)—marking the core noun that defines a named process, device or item.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on boundary‐marking symbols—i.e. punctuation or special characters that open or close segments (end‐of‐sentence dots, quotes/brackets in various scripts, C-style comment markers, replacement chars, etc.).

This feature fires on the tokens that kick off a new instruction or code‐structure element—whether an imperative verb in prose (“Find”, “How”), the punctuation introducing arguments or assignments (colons, “=”, “(”), or the identifier at the start of a declaration or function call (method names, parameter names, static association symbols, selector calls, etc.).

This neuron is a general “segment­-boundary” detector: it lights up on tokens that mark the end (or beginning) of a self‐contained unit—sentence-final punctuation (., Japanese full-stop, Greek/Russian periods, Chinese quotes), closing or opening delimiters (brackets, comment markers /*), hashtags/tags, file-extension dots, etc.

This feature fires on “atomic” labels in technical or structured contexts—things like numeric literals (e.g. 2, 13th, 50), code or locale codes (S, zh_CN), and identifier names or keys in JSON/code (Legend, SetCallBack, academic_term, MyCompany.Common). It flags tokens that act as standalone labels/identifiers rather than ordinary words.
This feature detects sentence-final full stops—especially the period ending boilerplate legal/license or document-header lines.

This feature detects the “lead‐in” entity or topic label of a factual statement—i.e. the proper name, role, place, version tag or other headline-style phrase that introduces the main subject of the sentence.
